newsitem.title: GERMANY: East German spymaster goes on trial for kidnapping.
newsitem.headline: East German spymaster goes on trial for kidnapping.

text.p: Legendary East German spymaster Markus Wolf went on trial on Tuesday charged with three Cold War kidnappings which could have come straight from the pages of a classic espionage thriller.
The trial is a last bid by prosecutors to bring Wolf to book after Germany's constitutional court in 1995 overturned a 1993 conviction for treason.
The supreme court said he could not be convicted for spying from East Berlin on what was then a foreign country -- West Germany.

This time prosecutors have charged the suave 73-year old with acts which were also illegal in East Germany -- abduction, coercion and causing bodily harm. The charges relate to East German intelligence operations in the 1950s and 1960s.

In 1962 an officer of the Ministry for State Security -- the feared East German secret police whose foreign intelligence operation Wolf founded and ran for three decades -- was demoted over a love affair frowned upon by his superiors.

The officer, Walter Thraene, fled to Austria. But Stasi officers lured him and his girlfriend to a hideout, beat him unconscious and spirited them back to East Berlin. Thraene spent over 10 years in jail, his girlfriend three.
Wolf denies having known of that operation, but his signature does appear on the 1955 order to try to recruit Christa Trapp, a German translator at the U.S. High Commission in West Berlin.
Trapp was abducted to East Berlin but refused to sign up as a spy and was sent home the next day.

And Wolf makes no secret of having ordered the detention in 1959 on fabricated charges of Georg Angerer, an East German typesetter who worked in Nazi-occupied Norway in World War Two as interpreter for the Gestapo secret police.
The aim was to make Angerer sign defamatory statements about Brandt, then mayor of West Berlin, who spent some time in Norway during the war.
